source: CARDI (2011), "Handbook of Integrated Techniques for Increasing Wet-Season and Dry-Season Rice Productivity" (Khmer, 50pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, foreword by H.E. Chan Sarun, Minister of Agriculture, dated 26 August 2011)
text: The insect pest causing the most frequent and severe damage to Cambodian rice is described in this source under a Khmer name transcribed as 'mmach ntaot' (planthopper), matching the biology of the brown planthopper (BPH): body about the size of a rice grain, amber/brown at the adult stage, life cycle about 35 days. Adult females mate soon after reaching adulthood and can lay up to about 500 eggs each, in clusters of 7–8 eggs arranged like a banana-hand, inserted into leaf-sheath tissue. Eggs hatch after about a week; nymphs pass through 5 molts over about 15 days before reaching adulthood. Most adults are short-winged, but long-winged adults appear and disperse by flight when the population needs to relocate to a new breeding/feeding site. Newly hatched through adult nymphs all feed on and damage the crop from seedbed to maturity, though damage from immature and adult stages is more severe than from newly hatched nymphs. Damage takes two forms: (1) direct feeding damage — heavy sap-sucking at the base of the plant causes the whole hill to dry out and die from the base upward ('hopperburn'); and (2) virus transmission — BPH is a vector for two rice virus diseases. Warm, humid, still air inside a dense canopy favors BPH buildup, so keeping the crop from becoming excessively dense (avoiding overly high seeding/planting density) helps prevent outbreaks, as does avoiding excess nitrogen fertilizer, which makes leaves and stems soft and succulent and easier for BPH to feed on and lay eggs in, encouraging faster population growth. Natural enemies that should be conserved in and around the field include spiders, dragonflies and damselflies, mirid bugs, hoverflies (syrphid flies) and crickets, all of which prey on BPH eggs and nymphs. Field scouting: inspect the seedbed and the transplanted/broadcast field from tillering to grain-filling at least once a week; if BPH is found, increase scouting to every 2–3 days. Action threshold: treat when the seedbed shows an average of 2–3 or more BPH per clump, or when the field shows 10 or more BPH (adults and nymphs combined) per 2 hills or per square meter. Integrated response, in order: if water is available, flood the field to submerge the base of the plants for about 7–8 days (leaving only the leaf tips exposed) to prevent BPH from feeding at the base and to stop eggs from hatching there; while flooded, sweep along the water surface with a fine mesh net to knock down and collect floating BPH nymphs and adults and destroy them. Where water is not available, chemical control becomes necessary: first spray a knockdown insecticide (BPMC, brand name Bassa) to kill adult BPH, then about a week later spray an insect growth regulator (buprofezin, brand name Applaud/Butyl) to prevent surviving nymphs from reaching adulthood; recommended dose depends on growth stage and water availability — roughly 30 g/tank (Bassa) for seedbeds without standing water, 35 g/tank with standing water, and 50–60 g/tank for transplanted/broadcast fields, versus roughly 3 g/tank (Butyl/Applaud) for seedbeds without water, 4 g/tank with water, and 5–8 g/tank for transplanted/broadcast fields (1 tank = 20 liters, applied at 360–400 liters of spray solution per hectare); never transplant seedlings from a seedbed that is already heavily infested with BPH nymphs. Resistant/tolerant varieties named in the source: IR Kesar, Chol'sa and K12 show medium resistance to BPH.
caveat: The Khmer pest name is transcribed phonetically from a scanned, encrypted PDF with imperfect font rendering; the exact standard Khmer spelling is uncertain and should be verified. The biology, damage pattern and virus-vector role described here match brown planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens) closely and align with the already-confirmed brown-planthopper/virus-vector entries from this project's separate CARDI-2007-book batches, so this should be duplicate-checked and likely merged with those rather than kept as a fully separate topic; what is new here is the specific action threshold, dosage table by growth stage/water availability, and the resistant-variety list (IR Kesar, Chol'sa, K12), which do not appear to be in the earlier confirmed entries. Insecticide active ingredients (BPMC/Bassa, buprofezin/Applaud-Butyl) and dosages are as printed in a 2011 source and should be checked against current label rates and current pesticide-availability/registration status before being given to farmers as advice.
